info.name: DK Payment Gateway — Business API
info.description:
Every endpoint the gateway exposes, grouped by who may call it.

THREE SURFACES, THREE CREDENTIALS.
• Public — no credential (health).
• Business — `X-API-Key`. This is what the booking service uses.
• Admin — a session cookie from Sign in, plus `X-CSRF-Token` on writes.

Run **Admin → Sign in** first: it captures the session cookie and the CSRF token into the environment, which every admin write below depends on.

WHAT 'UPSTREAM_UNAVAILABLE' MEANS. The gateway resolved your merchant, decrypted its credential and tried to reach the bank — which does not exist locally. Everything this service is responsible for worked. It is the expected result for a correctly-formed local call, not a failure.

DESTRUCTIVE REQUESTS ARE SKIPPED BY DEFAULT. Regenerate key, Disable credential and Sign out would each break the rest of the run — the first invalidates the very key the business calls use. Set `allow_destructive` to `true` in the environment to run them deliberately.

request.description: Liveness. The only endpoint that needs nothing at all.

item.name: 2 · Admin — session
item.description: Sign in first. The session cookie and CSRF token are captured automatically and every admin folder below depends on them. Sign out is deliberately the last folder in the collection, not here — running it early ends the session for everything after it.

request.description:
Signs in and captures the session cookie and CSRF token every admin request below depends on. Run it first.

THE CAPTCHA TOKEN. This gateway challenges every sign-in, including the first — LOGIN_CAPTCHA_AFTER_FAILURES defaults to 0 — so the password alone is refused with 400 'captcha required'.

Locally that is satisfied by any string, because development uses Cloudflare's published test secret, which accepts anything.

AGAINST A REAL DEPLOYMENT THIS REQUEST CANNOT WORK, and that is the captcha doing its job: a Turnstile token is issued to a browser that solved a challenge, and no collection can forge one. To exercise the admin API against a deployment, either sign in through the dashboard and copy the session cookie into this environment, or run the collection against an environment configured with the test keys. The business endpoints in folders 6 and 7 need no session — they authenticate with an API key and are unaffected.
Must be 401. Repeated failures lock the account — see LOGIN_MAX_ATTEMPTS.
Reads the signed-in admin back.
Every registered client. The booking service is one of these.
Returns the API key **once**, base64 and split by `**` markers. Strip the markers and base64-decode to get the usable `sk_live_...` key. It cannot be read again — regenerate if lost.

**Destructive — skipped unless `allow_destructive` is `true`.**

Invalidates the old key immediately. Anything using it stops working.

item.name: 4 · Admin — merchant routing
item.description: How the gateway decides whose money it is. A business call fails with MERCHANT_NOT_CONFIGURED until all three exist: a recipient, a mapping from your merchant reference to it, and an *active* credential for the provider.

request.description: Who ultimately receives the money.

exec: const b = pm.response.json(); if (b.data && b.data.recipient_id) { pm.environment.set('recipient_id', b.data.recipient_id); }

request.description:
Where this recipient's money lands. That is the whole record.

DKPG issues this gateway ONE identity — api_key, username, password, client_id, client_secret, source_app — and it is identical for every recipient, so it lives in the gateway's environment (DKPG_* variables), not here. Sending any of those keys is refused, not ignored: a record that appears to carry its own credentials, but does not use them, is worse than one that never claimed to.

beneficiary_bank is optional. It is only a fallback for the remitter's bank code, which the payer normally supplies.

Stripe is the other way round — see the request below. It onboards each merchant separately, so a Stripe record does carry that merchant's key.

Which sub-merchant this recipient's money is booked to. That is the whole record.

The same division as the DKPG request above. The provider knows this gateway as one agency under one key, so STRIPE_API_KEY and STRIPE_AGENCY_NAME live in the environment alongside STRIPE_BASE_URL. Sending either here is refused, not ignored.
A draft credential is not used. Activate it or routing still fails.
**Destructive — skipped unless `allow_destructive` is `true`.**

request.description:
Every property the booking platform knows, joined against what is routed here, so the gap is visible.

This gateway holds the bank details; the platform holds the properties. Neither can answer 'who cannot be paid yet' alone, which is how seven of eight properties stayed unconfigured without anything saying so.

app_id is REQUIRED. Routing is keyed on (app, merchant_reference) — two integrations may pay the same property into different accounts — so the question has no answer until one app is named. Without it: 400.

Needs the booking platform running (./dev/start.sh); otherwise connected is false and the tab says so rather than showing an empty table.

request.description: Card payments. Empty until one is made.

UPI payment records, read live from the booking platform.

No UPI money passes through this gateway — the guest pays the property's own account directly — so there is no transaction here to settle or refund. These are the records: the reference the guest gave, the number to ring them on, whether the property has approved it, and where the screenshot is.

This gateway holds none of it. It calls the booking platform server-side with a shared key (PLATFORM_API_KEY here, INTERNAL_API_KEY there) and passes the answer through. Nothing is cached.

`connected: false` with 502 means the booking platform could not be reached. That is a real failure and the dashboard shows it as one — it must never be mistaken for 'there are no UPI payments'.

Start the booking service (./dev/start.sh) before running this.

exec: pm.test('connected to the booking platform', () => pm.expect(body.connected).to.eql(true));
pm.test('carries the reference to search a bank for', () => pm.expect(row.transactionReference).to.be.a('string').and.not.empty);
pm.test('carries the property and the decision', () => {
pm.test('screenshot points at this gateway, not the platform', () => {

request.description:
The guest's own screenshot of the transfer, proxied from the booking platform.

A proxy rather than a redirect, so the shared key never reaches a browser. The reference is set by the request above; run that one first.

This is a file a stranger uploaded, served inside an administrative page, so the response is pinned down: only image/png or image/jpeg is accepted from the platform, and it comes back with `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff`, `Cache-Control: no-store` and `Content-Security-Policy: default-src 'none'; sandbox` — stricter than this site's own policy, and it is not overwritten by it.

item.name: 8 · Refusals worth checking
item.description: These must fail, and fail in the documented way.

request.description: The gateway will not move money it cannot attribute.
Minimum is 1.00 USD.
Admin writes require the CSRF header even with a valid session.

item.name: UPI screenshot for a booking that does not exist

request.description: 404, not an empty image and not a 403. A 403 would confirm the booking exists, which is the thing a stranger guessing references is trying to learn.

400, and the message names the offending key.

The bank knows one integrator, so authentication belongs to the gateway, not to a recipient. Accepting these fields and then ignoring them would let somebody believe one hotel pays through credentials of its own.
400, naming api_key. The card provider knows one agency under one key; a recipient record says only which sub-merchant it is.

400. Routing is per app, so without one named there is no single answer. An earlier version collapsed the apps and showed whichever mapping came last — a screen that could name the wrong bank account with complete confidence. It refuses now.
